title: Why is using a `HashSet` for the lookup list (`filter(set::contains)`) faster than `filter(list::contains)` for intersection queries?
shortTitle: Why is using a HashSet for the lookup list faster than filter(list::contains) for intersection queries?

s1_definition.profdef: `List.contains` scans linearly, O(m) per call, so filtering n elements against a list is O(n·m). `HashSet.contains` is O(1) average, so filtering against a set is O(n), a major speed-up for intersection.
s1_definition.analogy: Checking a name against a plain list means reading the whole list each time; checking against a hash set is like a direct index lookup — instant.
s1_definition.oneliner: `list::contains` is O(n·m); `set::contains` is O(n) — build a HashSet for lookups.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `List.contains` scans linearly, O(m) per call, so filtering n elements against a list is O(n·m). `HashSet.contains` is O(1) average, so filtering against a set is O(n), a major speed-up for intersection.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Checking a name against a plain list means reading the whole list each time; checking against a hash set is like a direct index lookup — instant.

**One line to remember:** `list::contains` is O(n·m); `set::contains` is O(n) — build a HashSet for lookups.

sections.s2_technical:
`ArrayList.contains` walks the list comparing each element, costing O(m) per check. In an intersection, you call contains for each of the n outer elements, so the total is O(n·m). `HashSet.contains` computes the hash and probes one bucket, averaging O(1), so the whole filter is O(n).

The fix is to build a HashSet of the lookup collection once, outside the stream, and filter with `set::contains`. For large m this is the difference between a slow quadratic scan and a fast linear pass. The HashSet relies on correct hashCode and equals.

The senior nuance is that this is the canonical optimisation for membership and intersection: materialise the lookup side into a HashSet first. The one-time cost of building the set, O(m), is dwarfed by the savings when n is non-trivial. For custom element types, hashCode and equals must be correct and consistent or the set degrades. Recognising the quadratic cost of list-contains in a loop is the key insight.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — An intersection at the National Bank of India finds accounts present in both a large active list and a large flagged list, and list-contains made it crawl.

This is exactly the HashSet-lookup optimisation — building a set turns the quadratic scan into a linear pass.

The code contrasts list-contains with set-contains in an `IntersectionService.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: twenty active ids and a flagged list of four ids.

Step 1: The slow version, for each of the twenty ids, scans the whole flagged list to check membership.

Step 2: It returns the four matches, but at twenty times four comparisons that scale as the product of the sizes.

Step 3: The fast version builds a HashSet of the flagged ids once.

Step 4: It then checks each active id with a constant-time contains, returning the same four matches in linear time.

```
INFO: list::contains  (O(n*m)): [3, 7, 11, 15]
INFO: set::contains   (O(n))  : [3, 7, 11, 15]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  active (n) ∩ flagged (m)
    slow: for each active → scan flagged list (O(m)) → O(n*m)
    fast: Set(flagged) once (O(m)) → filter(set::contains O(1)) → O(n)
```

  │  + fast(...): List                 │ Set + filter(set::contains) O(n)

  2. filter(flaggedSet::contains).toList()

sections.s6_takeaway:
The difference is the cost of the membership check. A list's contains scans the list linearly, costing order m per call, so filtering n elements against a list is order n times m — quadratic when both sides are large. A HashSet's contains computes the hash and probes a single bucket, averaging constant time, so filtering against a set is order n overall. That is the entire reason the set version is faster for intersection.

So the canonical fix is to materialise the lookup side into a HashSet once, outside the stream, and filter with set contains. At the National Bank of India an intersection of a large active list against a large flagged list went from crawling to fast purely by building that set first — the one-time cost of building it, order m, is dwarfed by the savings when n is non-trivial.

The senior point I stress is recognising the hidden quadratic cost of calling list contains inside a filter, and that the HashSet depends on correct and consistent hashCode and equals for the element type — if those are wrong, the set degrades toward linear probing and the benefit evaporates. For any membership or intersection query over sizable data, building a HashSet for the lookup side is the first optimisation I reach for.
